frames.narration: A run-length encoder turns aaab into 3a1b. It has a bug: a run of 10 or more equal characters is written wrongly. Five hand-written examples all pass, because the longest run in them is 9.

The property: decode(encode(s)) must equal s. The generator makes strings of up to 20 uniform letters from a to z. After 1,000 cases there is no failure. A run of 10 equal letters out of 26 is almost never generated.

Narrow the alphabet to a and b. Runs are far more likely, and with seed 101 the property fails at case 845, on a 15-character string. A different seed fails at case 72 instead: the luck changes, the reach does not.
A generator biased toward repeating the previous character does better still: the failure is found at case 2, on a 19-character input. Shaping the generator beat running many more blind cases.

A 19-character failure is hard to read. The shrinker deletes one character at a time, keeping any smaller input that still fails. It ends at 10 identical characters, aaaaaaaaaa, in 9 steps. The cause is plain: the bug starts at a run of 10.
The seed makes it repeatable: running seed 101 again gives the same case and the same minimal input, so the failure can be replayed on any machine. Without the seed the failure would be a ghost.

Now the weak property: the encoded text is not empty when the input is not. It holds for every input, so 1,000 cases pass with the bug still in place. A green run from a property that cannot fail proves nothing.
